Executive Summary
This study addresses the challenge of synthesizing air-stable organic radicals for photothermal applications. The authors designed and synthesized a series of star-shaped aromatic nitric acid radicals (ANARs) by demethylating phenolic precursors in air. Unlike traditional radicals that are kinetically unstable, these ANARs exhibit high thermal and electrochemical stability due to rich resonance structures. The research demonstrates that high spin concentration in these materials leads to restricted radiative decay, significantly enhancing nonradiative heat generation. Among the synthesized compounds, TPA-TPA-O6 emerged as the superior candidate, displaying broad absorption from 300 to 2000 nm and negligible photobleaching. In solar-driven water evaporation tests, TPA-TPA-O6 achieved a record-breaking efficiency of 89.41% and an evaporation rate of 1.293 kg/m²h under one sun, outperforming many inorganic and organic counterparts. The material also showed excellent stability over ten laser cycles and potential for seawater desalination, offering a low-cost, reproducible strategy for high-performance organic photothermal materials.

Research Context
Open-shell radicals are typically unstable in air due to unsatisfied valency. Organic small molecules are often overlooked compared to inorganic or polymer materials. Existing organic dyes suffer from cumbersome synthesis and poor stability. Stable neutral radicals are rare and challenging to prepare. Photothermal materials convert NIR light into heat via nonradiative decay.

Research Question And Hypothesis
Can stable aromatic nitric acid radicals be synthesized without steric protection? Do these radicals exhibit high spin concentration and restricted radiative decay? Will high spin concentration enhance photothermal conversion efficiency? Can TPA-TPA-O6 achieve top-tier performance in solar water evaporation? Does the radical structure enable efficient seawater desalination?

Methodological Details
Four star-shaped ANAR materials were synthesized via demethylation and oxidation. Precursors were phenolic hydroxyl compounds with different cores. Synthesis involved demethylation followed by oxidation in air. Cyclic voltammetry was used to assess electrochemical stability. UV-vis absorption was measured in dichloromethane solution and film. PLQY was tested in solution and film to confirm radical formation. ESR spectra were recorded at 0.02 mmol to quantify spin concentration. Photothermal properties were evaluated using an 808 nm laser. Water evaporation was tested using a polyurethane foam interface. Seawater desalination was verified by ion concentration analysis.

Procedures And Architectures
Demethylation converts methoxy precursors to radical species. HOMO levels were calculated based on CV curves. HOMO levels for TPA-TPA-O6 were measured at -4.90 eV. Radicals showed negligible fluorescence due to nonradiative decay. High spin concentration was confirmed by ESR signal intensity. Temperature was monitored using an IR thermal camera. Laser power was increased to 1.0 W cm-2 for stability testing. PU foam was impregnated with TPA-TPA-O6 solution and dried. Evaporation rate was calculated from mass change curves.

Key Results
TPA-TPA-O6 showed broad absorption from 300 to 2000 nm. TPA-TPA-O6 reached 210 °C within 60 seconds under 0.8 W/cm². TPA-TPA-O6 maintained stability for ten laser cycles. Equilibrium temperature reached 81.2 °C under continuous irradiation. Water evaporation efficiency achieved 89.41% under one sun. Water evaporation rate reached 1.293 kg/m²h. Ion concentrations were significantly reduced in seawater. TPA-TPA-O6 showed negligible photobleaching effect. PLQY of TPA-TPA-O6 was 0.1% in the solid state. Temperature rose to 250 °C at 1.0 W/cm² laser power.

Interpretation And Theoretical Implications
High spin concentration drives nonradiative decay. Restricted radiative decay enhances photothermal conversion. Resonance structures ensure air stability. Broad absorption facilitates sunlight harvesting. Organic radicals offer a novel design strategy. Low cost and simple synthesis enable scalability. Future work will focus on enhanced planarity.

Contradictions And Limitations
Some radicals showed lower ESR signal due to lower HOMO. TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 had poor photothermal performance. Partial protonation may affect performance in some cores.

TPA-TPA-O6 is superior to other ANARs and organic materials. exhibits the highest photothermal conversion performance exhibit extremely wide absorption spectra water evaporation efficiency of 89.41% TPA-TPZ-O6 and TPA-PY-O8 limit their photothermal conversion performance. promising practical application potential in future

Data And Code Availability
Supporting Information is available free of charge at http://pubs.acs.org.

Robustness And Ablation Notes
TPA-TPA-O6 showed excellent stability for ten cycles. Temperature rose regularly with laser intensity.

Ethical Considerations
Organic materials avoid heavy metal ion poisoning.

Key Figures Tables
Figure 1 shows the synthetic scheme and structures. Figure 2 shows UV-Vis absorption spectra. Figure 3 shows cyclic voltammetry curves. Figure 4 shows ESR and PLQY results. Figure 5 shows temperature increment under laser. Figure 6 shows evaporation system and efficiency.

Three Takeaways
1. Stable aromatic nitric acid radicals enable high-efficiency photothermal conversion. 2. TPA-TPA-O6 achieved 89.41% efficiency and 1.293 kg/m²h rate. 3. Future work will focus on enhanced planarity for electronics.
